# Before you start

This document is a self-contained tutorial. Every number and figure below is
produced by the code in the document, so you can **knit it on your own
computer** (RStudio: *Knit* button, or `rmarkdown::render("RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd")`)
and obtain the same results. Knitting takes about two minutes on a laptop.

**In the lecture** the slides follow this file in order. Each code slide names
the chunk to run (e.g. `fit-bt`); the slides show exactly the code in this
file, so your numbers and figures will match the ones on the screen. In
RStudio, run a chunk with the green arrow or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter, and use
*Run All Chunks Above* if you fall behind.

**Installation (run once).** RBBayes contains a little C++ code, so you need
the standard R build tools: Rtools on Windows, or the Xcode command-line tools
on macOS (`xcode-select --install` in a terminal).

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("remotes", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
remotes::install_github("lapo-santi/RBBayes")

# Optional, used in a few sections (each is skipped if not installed):
install.packages(c("coda", "bayesplot", "salso"))
```

A copy of this file is installed with the package:

```{r tutorial-path, eval = FALSE}
file.copy(system.file("tutorial", "RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd", package = "RBBayes"), ".")
```

```{r packages}
library(RBBayes)
library(ggplot2)
has_coda      <- requireNamespace("coda", quietly = TRUE)
has_bayesplot <- requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE)
```

**What you will do.** We analyse two pairwise-comparison datasets:

1. a **synthetic tennis league** whose true tiers we know, so we can check what
   the models recover;
2. a **real season of ATP men's tennis** (2017), bundled with the package.

For each, we first *explore the data*, then fit a standard Bradley--Terry (BT)
model and a Bradley--Terry stochastic block model (BT--SBM). A short final
section shows the same workflow for **rankings** with the Plackett--Luce model.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $n$; $i, j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ | number of items (players); item indices |
| $y_{ij}$ | number of wins of $i$ over $j$ |
| $n_{ij} = y_{ij} + y_{ji}$ | number of comparisons between $i$ and $j$ |
| $\lambda_i > 0$ | strength of item $i$ in the standard BT model |
| $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ | block (tier) membership of item $i$ in the BT--SBM |
| $\lambda_k > 0$ | strength shared by all items in block $k$ |
| $K$ | number of occupied blocks |

The BT model says
$$
y_{ij} \mid \lambda \sim \operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(n_{ij}, \frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i + \lambda_j}\right),
$$
and the BT--SBM simply replaces $\lambda_i$ by $\lambda_{z_i}$: players in the
same block share one strength, so they beat each other with probability 1/2.

# Dataset 1: a synthetic tennis league

## Simulate the data

Twenty fictional players are split into four tiers of five players. Players in
a tier share a strength; the strengths are `12, 6, 2, 1`. Each pair plays 20
matches.

```{r simulate}
true_strength <- c(12, 6, 2, 1)
edges <- tennis_tiered_toy(
  n_blocks = 4, latent_strength = true_strength,
  players_per_block = 5, matches_per_pair = 20,
  seed = 101, format = "edgelist"
)
truth <- attr(edges, "truth")   # true tier and strength of each player
head(edges)
```

The data are an **edge list**: one row per (winner, loser) pair, with the
number of wins in `count`. `as_bt_data()` turns it into the win-count matrix
used by every fitting function.

```{r as-bt-data}
tennis <- as_bt_data(edges, count = "count")
tennis
tennis$wins[1:5, 1:5]      # wins[i, j] = wins of row player i over column player j
```

**Are the true strengths on the scale of the prior?** Below we give every
strength a Gamma(`shape_lambda` = 2, `rate_lambda` = $e^{\psi(2)}$) prior; this rate makes
$E[\log \lambda] = 0$, so a typical strength is about 1. Only ratios of strengths
matter, so compare the *ratios* $12/1$ with what the prior finds plausible:

```{r prior-scale}
shape_lambda <- 2
rate_lambda  <- exp(digamma(shape_lambda))
prior_draws  <- rgamma(1e5, shape = shape_lambda, rate = rate_lambda)
quantile(prior_draws, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
# Ratio of the 95% to the 5% prior quantile versus the largest true ratio:
c(prior_ratio = unname(quantile(prior_draws, 0.95) / quantile(prior_draws, 0.05)),
  true_ratio  = max(true_strength) / min(true_strength))
```

The true strength ratio is within the range the prior considers plausible. A
generating vector such as `c(64, 16, 4, 1)` would put the strongest tier far in
the prior's tail, and would also make the example unrealistically easy.

## Explore the data first

Before fitting anything, look at the raw outcomes.

```{r eda-table}
n_ij <- tennis$wins + t(tennis$wins)
player_table <- data.frame(
  player  = tennis$item_labels,
  matches = rowSums(n_ij),
  wins    = rowSums(tennis$wins)
)
player_table$win_rate <- round(player_table$wins / player_table$matches, 3)
player_table <- player_table[order(-player_table$win_rate), ]
rownames(player_table) <- NULL
head(player_table, 8)
c(players = tennis$n_items,
  pairs_compared = sum(n_ij[upper.tri(n_ij)] > 0),
  matches = sum(tennis$wins))
```

```{r eda-winrate, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(player_table, aes(x = win_rate, y = reorder(player, win_rate))) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Overall win rate", y = NULL,
       title = "Overall win rate of each player") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The win rates already suggest groups of players, but the gaps are not clean.

```{r eda-matrix, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_pairwise_outcomes(tennis)
```

Both axes use the same (random) player order, so no structure is visible yet.
Keep this picture in mind: after fitting the block model we will redraw it
with players ordered by their estimated tier.

## The standard Bradley--Terry model

Each player gets their own strength $\lambda_i \overset{iid}{\sim}$ Gamma(`shape_lambda`, `rate_lambda`).
In `bt_model()` you only give `shape_lambda` and `rate_lambda`.

```{r fit-bt}
bt_fit <- fit_model(
  tennis,
  bt_model(shape_lambda = 2, rate_lambda = exp(digamma(2))),
  mcmc_control(iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 12)
)
bt_fit
summary(bt_fit)
```

`iter` counts all iterations, `warmup` of them are discarded, and the remaining
`iter - warmup` draws are kept.

### Relative strengths

The likelihood only depends on ratios $\lambda_i/\lambda_j$, so we report the
**relative strength** of each player: their share of the total strength in each
draw, $\lambda_i / \sum_j \lambda_j$. Shares add to one; the dashed line marks
$1/n$, the share every player would have if all were equal.

```{r bt-strength, fig.height = 6}
plot_strength_summary(bt_fit)
```

```{r bt-ranks, fig.height = 6}
plot_rank_intervals(bt_fit)
```

### Who is stronger than whom? $\Pr(\lambda_i > \lambda_j \mid y)$

Rankings hide how sure we are about each comparison. `prob_stronger()` returns,
for every pair, the posterior probability that the row player is stronger than
the column player.

```{r bt-prob-stronger, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 8.5}
p_bt <- prob_stronger(bt_fit)
round(p_bt[1:5, 1:5], 2)
plot_prob_stronger(bt_fit)
```

The colour scale is centred at 0.5: white cells are pairs the data cannot
separate. Under the standard BT model, players from the same true tier often
have probabilities between 0.2 and 0.8 --- the model gives them distinct
strengths but cannot say which one is larger.

### Checking the MCMC

Convergence checks use the same relative strengths. Columns are named after
the players, e.g. `rel_strength[Kira Lane]`.

```{r bt-matrix}
draws <- as.matrix(bt_fit)
dim(draws)
colnames(draws)[1:4]
top_players <- paste0("rel_strength[", head(strength_summary(bt_fit)$item, 4), "]")
top_players
```

```{r bt-coda, eval = has_coda}
chain <- coda::as.mcmc(bt_fit)
round(coda::effectiveSize(chain)[top_players])
```

```{r bt-bayesplot, eval = has_bayesplot, fig.height = 4}
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(bt_fit, pars = top_players[1:2])
bayesplot::mcmc_intervals(bt_fit, pars = top_players, prob = 0.5, prob_outer = 0.95)
```

A single chain cannot reveal every problem. Run a second, independent chain
with a different seed and compare:

```{r bt-two-chains, eval = has_coda}
bt_fit2 <- fit_model(tennis, bt_fit$model,
                     mcmc_control(iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 112))
chains <- as_mcmc_chains(list(bt_fit, bt_fit2))
coda::gelman.diag(chains[, top_players], autoburnin = FALSE, multivariate = FALSE)
```

Values of the potential scale reduction factor close to 1 are reassuring.

## The Bradley--Terry stochastic block model

The BT--SBM groups players into blocks: $z_i$ is the block of player $i$,
$\lambda_k \overset{iid}{\sim}$ Gamma(`shape_lambda`, `rate_lambda`) is the strength of block $k$,
and the partition $z$ gets a prior that leaves the number of blocks $K$ random.

### Prior on the number of blocks

Before seeing data, how many blocks does each partition prior expect among
$n = 20$ players?

```{r prior-K}
priors <- list(
  Gnedin       = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5),
  DP           = dirichlet_process_prior(concentration = 1),
  PitmanYor    = pitman_yor_prior(concentration = 1, discount = 0.2),
  DirMult_max4 = dirichlet_multinomial_prior(max_clusters = 4, concentration = 1)
)
data.frame(
  prior        = names(priors),
  prior_mean_K = round(sapply(priors, function(p) prior_mean_K(20, p)), 2),
  row.names    = NULL
)
# Prior standard deviations are available for the Gnedin and DP priors:
sqrt(c(Gnedin = prior_variance_K(20, priors$Gnedin),
       DP     = prior_variance_K(20, priors$DP)))
```

We use the Gnedin prior, which allows a random but finite number of blocks
and, with its large prior standard deviation, is not very informative about $K$.

### Fit

```{r fit-sbm}
sbm_model <- bt_sbm_model(
  shape_lambda = 2, rate_lambda = exp(digamma(2)),
  item_clustering = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)
)
sbm_model
sbm_fit <- fit_model(tennis, sbm_model,
                     mcmc_control(iter = 10000, warmup = 5000, seed = 2))
summary(sbm_fit)
```

In a block model, individual strengths are not the natural summary (players
in a block share one value, and block labels change between draws), so the
summary reports the number of blocks and the estimated partition instead.

### How many blocks?

```{r K-table}
posterior_K_table(sbm_fit)
```

The truth, $K = 4$, is the most probable value, but there is real posterior
mass on 5 or more blocks: with strengths 12 vs 6 and 2 vs 1 the tiers are not
perfectly separated by 20 matches per pair.

```{r K-trace, fig.height = 3}
plot_mcmc_traces(sbm_fit)
```

### The estimated partition and the reordered data

`partition_point_estimate()` summarises the posterior over partitions by the
partition minimising the posterior expected variation of information (VI).
Block 1 is the strongest. Compare with the truth:

```{r z-hat}
z_hat <- partition_point_estimate(sbm_fit)
table(estimated_block = z_hat,
      true_tier = truth$true_block[match(names(z_hat), truth$item)])
```

Now redraw the outcome matrix with players ordered by their estimated block:

```{r ordered-adjacency, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_ordered_adjacency(sbm_fit, z_hat = z_hat, clean_fun = NULL)
```

The block structure that was invisible in the raw matrix is now obvious.

### Membership probabilities

`plot_assignment_probabilities()` shows, for each player, the posterior
probability of belonging to each block, **conditional on a given number of
blocks** $K$ (block labels are only comparable across draws with the same $K$).
The colour scale is centred at 0.5: blue means "more likely than not".

```{r assign-K4, fig.height = 6}
plot_assignment_probabilities(sbm_fit, k_show = 4, clean_fun = NULL)
```

Given $K = 4$, every draw has the same partition (the true one), so all
probabilities are 0 or 1. This does **not** mean the partition is certain: about
40% of the draws have more than four blocks, and they are excluded here. Look
at the draws with five blocks:

```{r assign-K5, fig.height = 6}
plot_assignment_probabilities(sbm_fit, k_show = 5, clean_fun = NULL)
```

With five blocks, one of the true tiers is split into two sub-blocks. Any tier
can be split, most often the middle ones (strengths 6 and 2), so several
players have probabilities between 0.2 and 0.8: white-ish cells mark players
whose sub-block is genuinely uncertain.

### Which players belong together?

The posterior similarity matrix does not condition on $K$: cell $(i, j)$ is
$\Pr(z_i = z_j \mid y)$, the proportion of all draws in which the two players
share a block. Outlines show the estimated partition.

```{r psm, fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 8.5}
plot_posterior_similarity(sbm_fit)
```

Within each outlined block the probabilities are around 0.85--0.97, and they
are **zero** outside. Where does the missing probability go? Not to other
blocks: in the draws where two players of the same tier are separated, the
tier has been split into sub-blocks. `block_stability()` makes this explicit:

```{r block-stability}
block_stability(sbm_fit, z_hat)[, c("block", "size", "together", "split", "merged")]
```

`merged` is zero for every block: no draw ever puts players from different
estimated blocks together. All the uncertainty is about splitting tiers, which
is exactly what the $K = 5$ membership plot showed.

### Credible ball for the partition

A credible ball (Wade & Ghahramani, 2018) is the smallest VI ball around
$\hat z$ that contains 95% of the posterior draws. Its bounds describe the
coarsest and finest partitions that remain plausible.

```{r credible-ball, fig.height = 6}
cb <- credible_ball(sbm_fit, z_hat = z_hat, credible_mass = 0.95)
cb
plot_credible_ball(cb)
```

If the GitHub package `mcclust.ext` is installed,
`credible_ball(sbm_fit, method = "mcclust.ext")` computes the same summary with
Wade's reference implementation.

### $\Pr(\lambda_i > \lambda_j \mid y)$ in the block model

```{r sbm-prob-stronger, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 8.5}
plot_prob_stronger(sbm_fit)
```

Compare with the standard BT model: between tiers the block model is close to
certain, while within a tier the two players are usually *tied*
($\lambda_{z_i} = \lambda_{z_j}$), so both $\Pr(\lambda_i > \lambda_j)$ and
$\Pr(\lambda_j > \lambda_i)$ are small. The tie probability is stored in the
`prob_equal` attribute and equals the posterior similarity:

```{r sbm-ties}
p_sbm <- prob_stronger(sbm_fit)
round(attr(p_sbm, "prob_equal")[1:5, 1:5], 2)
```

### A second chain

```{r sbm-chain2}
sbm_fit2 <- fit_model(tennis, sbm_model,
                      mcmc_control(iter = 10000, warmup = 5000, seed = 202))
merge(posterior_K_table(sbm_fit)[, c("K", "probability")],
      posterior_K_table(sbm_fit2)[, c("K", "probability")],
      by = "K", all = TRUE, suffixes = c("_chain1", "_chain2"))
```

Similar block-count distributions in independent chains are one useful (but
not sufficient) check of convergence.

# Dataset 2: the 2017 ATP season

The package includes head-to-head counts for the 105 top ATP players in each
season from 2000 to 2025.

## Explore the data

```{r atp-load}
atp <- ATP_2000_2025[["2017"]]
players <- atp$players_df
atp_data <- as_bt_data(atp$Y_ij, item_labels = make.unique(players$player_label))
atp_data
```

```{r atp-eda}
n_ij <- atp$N_ij
c(players = nrow(n_ij),
  matches = sum(atp$Y_ij),
  pairs_that_met = sum(n_ij[upper.tri(n_ij)] > 0),
  possible_pairs = choose(nrow(n_ij), 2))
```

Unlike the synthetic league, most pairs never met: only about one pair in
four played each other. The model borrows strength through common opponents.

```{r atp-eda-plots, fig.height = 4}
atp_players <- data.frame(
  player = atp_data$item_labels,
  matches = rowSums(n_ij),
  win_rate = rowSums(atp$Y_ij) / rowSums(n_ij),
  year_end_rank = players$last_rank
)
ggplot(atp_players, aes(matches)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#0072B2", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Matches against other top-105 players", y = "Players") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(atp_players, aes(year_end_rank, win_rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = matches), alpha = 0.6, colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Year-end ATP ranking (log scale)", y = "Win rate",
       size = "Matches") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Win rate falls with ranking, but noisily, especially for players with few
matches.

## Fit the BT--SBM

```{r atp-fit}
atp_fit <- fit_model(
  atp_data,
  bt_sbm_model(shape_lambda = 2, rate_lambda = exp(digamma(2)),
               item_clustering = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)),
  mcmc_control(iter = 6000, warmup = 3000, seed = 1)
)
posterior_K_table(atp_fit)
```

The number of tiers is much less certain than in the synthetic league.

```{r atp-zhat}
atp_z <- partition_point_estimate(atp_fit)
table(atp_z)
names(atp_z)[atp_z == 1]          # the top tier
```

```{r atp-adjacency, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 9}
plot_ordered_adjacency(atp_fit, z_hat = atp_z, clean_fun = NULL)
```

Do the estimated tiers agree with the official rankings?

```{r atp-vs-ranking, fig.height = 4}
atp_players$block <- factor(atp_z[atp_players$player])
ggplot(atp_players, aes(block, year_end_rank)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Estimated block (1 = strongest)", y = "Year-end ATP ranking (log)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Uncertainty about the tiers

```{r atp-cb}
atp_cb <- credible_ball(atp_fit, z_hat = atp_z)
atp_cb
block_stability(atp_fit, atp_z)[, c("block", "size", "together", "split", "merged")]
```

The 95% credible ball ranges from three to about ten blocks. Unlike the
synthetic example, the estimated blocks are almost never reproduced exactly:
`split` and `merged` are both close to one for the two large blocks, meaning
that the boundary between lower tiers moves from draw to draw and players
cross it. Even the top tier is reproduced exactly in only about half of the
draws; in the others, further players join it.

Membership probabilities for the most probable number of blocks:

```{r atp-assign, fig.height = 14, fig.width = 7}
plot_assignment_probabilities(atp_fit, clean_fun = NULL)
```

## Who is stronger than whom among the top players?

```{r atp-prob-stronger, fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 8.5}
plot_prob_stronger(atp_fit, max_items = 15)
```

Federer and Nadal are tied in most draws (they share the top block), so
neither is "stronger" than the other with high probability. Below them, many
probabilities sit between 0.1 and 0.45: these players share blocks in some
draws and not in others. A player with few matches against the top 105 (look
up Krajinović in `atp_players`) can have a high posterior mean but large
uncertainty.

# Rankings: the Plackett--Luce model

Rankings record items in order of preference rather than pairwise outcomes.
The Plackett--Luce (PL) model chooses the first item with probability
proportional to its strength, then the second among those remaining, and so on.
For a first analysis we use the standard model, with one strength per item.

```{r pl-data, fig.height = 5}
sushi <- sushi_toy(n_rankings = 40, rank_length = 5, seed = 3)
sushi
head(sushi$rankings, 3)
plot_ranking_positions(sushi)
```

```{r pl-fit}
pl_fit <- fit_model(sushi, pl_model(shape_lambda = 1, rate_lambda = 1),
                    mcmc_control(iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, seed = 4))
summary(pl_fit)
```

As for BT, reported strengths are shares of total strength in each draw.

```{r pl-strength, fig.height = 5}
plot_strength_summary(pl_fit)
```

```{r pl-prob-stronger, fig.height = 6.5, fig.width = 8}
plot_prob_stronger(pl_fit)
```

The same `fit_model()` call also fits PL models with item blocks
(`pl_sbm_model()`), groups of rankers (`pl_mixture_model()`) or both
(`pl_lbm_model()`); see `vignette("pl-ranking-models", package = "RBBayes")`.

# Exercises

1. Simulate the synthetic league with `latent_strength = c(12, 9, 2, 1)`. How do
   the posterior of $K$ and the credible ball change? What does
   `block_stability()` now report?
2. Reduce `matches_per_pair` to 5. Which summaries change most?
3. Refit the ATP season with `gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.8)` and with
   `dirichlet_process_prior(concentration = 1)`. Compare `prior_mean_K()` and
   `posterior_K_table()` for the two priors.
4. Choose another ATP season (e.g. `"2008"` or `"2023"`). Is the top tier
   larger or smaller than in 2017?
